unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4: Transport, Cities, and Urban Solutions! In this unit you will explore how cities grow, how people move through them, and how communities around the world are finding creative solutions to make urban life better for everyone. You will read about transport systems, green innovations, and the challenges that cities face in East Africa and beyond.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary file. Learn a few words each day and add them to your Word Wall.
Work through the lessons in the Grammar file (Prepositions, Passive Voice, Comparatives, Sentence Adverbs).
Read the Story file, "A Heart in the Noise", and answer the comprehension questions.
Come back to this lesson file and work through all nine sections in order.
Finish with the Check Your Learning self-assessment at the end.

readings.title: Moving Through Mogadishu: A City in Motion
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every morning at 6:30, the streets of Mogadishu begin to hum with life. Minibuses crowd the main roads, motorcycles weave between cars, and pedestrians walk quickly along dusty pavements. For the people of this growing East African capital, getting from one place to another is both a daily challenge and a daily adventure.
Mogadishu is one of the fastest-growing cities in East Africa. Its population has fluctuated dramatically over the past two decades, rising as people move in from rural areas searching for work, education, and safety. The city's roads, many of which were damaged in years of conflict, are now being rebuilt. New tarmac is laid every month, and traffic lights have been installed at several busy junctions. But the city is growing faster than its infrastructure can keep up.
The most common forms of public transport are the minibus and the three-wheeled bajaaj. These vehicles are often painted in bright colours and decorated with stickers and patterns. They follow no fixed timetable — they leave when they are full. For passengers, this means that journey times can fluctuate from twenty minutes to over an hour, depending on the traffic and the number of stops.
At the Bakaaraha market, one of the largest open-air markets in East Africa, the streets become even more crowded. Traders push carts loaded with vegetables, electronics, and fabrics. Donkey carts carry heavy goods through narrow lanes. The arrangement of stalls looks haphazard to a visitor, but regular shoppers know exactly where to find what they need.
Young people in Mogadishu are thinking about how to improve urban transport. A group of university students recently proposed a simple bus-route map that could be shared on mobile phones. Their idea is that if passengers know which route a bus follows and when it is likely to arrive, travel will become faster and safer. "The city should be made easier to navigate," said Nadir, one of the students. "Better information can be given to everyone."
Other cities in East Africa are already experimenting with solutions. In Nairobi, a digital mapping project has been created by young engineers. In Dar es Salaam, a new rapid-bus system was built to reduce traffic. These projects show that transport problems can be solved when communities work together and young people are encouraged to share their ideas.
Unfortunately, many cities still struggle with pollution from old vehicles, dangerous roads for pedestrians, and overcrowded buses. But there is also reason for hope. Certainly, the energy and creativity of young East Africans are making a difference. As Nadir puts it: "A city should not just be built for cars. It should be designed for people."
Mogadishu is louder, busier, and more exuberant than it has been in years. The city is not perfect, but it is alive — and the young people who move through its streets every day are determined to make it better.

readings.title: An Interview About City Transport
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every city is really thousands of small journeys happening at once. To understand how Mogadishu moves, a student reporter from the school newsletter interviewed Amara, a commuter who crosses the city every day to reach her college classes. Her answers show how ordinary passengers experience the roads — and how much thought young people already give to improving them.
Reporter: Tell us about transport in your city.
Amara: I live in Mogadishu. The main way to get around is by minibus or bajaaj. The buses are always full, especially in the morning and at about 5 p.m., when people are going home from work. If you want a seat, you learn to arrive early, greet the driver, and wait your turn. Passengers help each other with bags and parcels, and regular riders know every stop by heart.
Reporter: What is the biggest problem with transport?
Amara: Unfortunately, the roads are sometimes in bad condition. There are potholes and dust, and in the rainy season some roads flood completely. Also, there are no printed maps or timetables, so you never know exactly when the bus will come. The waiting time can fluctuate from a few minutes to nearly an hour, and that makes people late for work and school.
Reporter: Do you ever walk instead?
Amara: I walk the last kilometre every day, because the minibus cannot enter our narrow street. Walking is slower than riding, but it is calmer, and I notice things — a new shop opening, a repaired wall, a neighbour to greet. My brother cycles to the port where he works, and he says he is wary at the big junctions, where drivers turn without looking. That is why protected cycle lanes matter.
Reporter: How could transport be improved?
Amara: I think better roads should be built, and a clear bus timetable should be created. Cycling lanes would help too, because cycling is cheaper than taking the bus and better for the environment. Certainly, young people have many ideas about how to make the city better. Students at the university have already drawn a route map that can be shared on mobile phones.
Reporter: What advice do you have for visitors?
Amara: Be patient! The traffic can be slow, but the city is more exciting than you might expect. Walk through the markets, try the food, and talk to people. Ask a regular passenger which minibus to take, because local knowledge beats any map. Mogadishu is busier and more vibrant than ever before.
One commuter cannot speak for a whole city, of course. But planners across East Africa agree on this much: transport improves fastest when the people who ride the buses every day are asked what they actually need. Every timetable, every repaired road and every new cycle lane starts the same way — with somebody's ordinary journey, described honestly.

readings.title: A Heart in the Noise, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
In the dusty lanes of Mwananyamala, on the edge of Dar es Salaam, the air was always full — of smoke from the chapati stalls, music from the boda bodas, and voices rising in greeting or complaint. Life moved quickly. Sometimes too quickly.
Thirteen-year-old Imani stood in front of the community kiosk where her mother sold phone credit and chewing gum. Her shoulders slumped as she stared at her crumpled maths test. A red "37%" was circled at the top. Her teacher's comment — "You must improve your discipline" — rang in her ears.
Around her, the world buzzed with the exuberant energy of boys playing football. It made her sadness feel heavier. Their laughter sounded like a cruel echo. She stuffed the paper into her backpack. Unfortunately, she had no words for how embarrassed she felt.
At home, her father was cleaning his tools. He repaired shoes in a small open workshop beside the house. He looked up as she walked past. "How was school, Imani?" "Fine," she muttered. He noticed something in her voice and frowned, but said nothing.
The truth was that Imani had stopped studying weeks ago. She did not know why. Maybe it was the noise at home. Maybe it was the way her phone could tempt her to scroll instead of revising. Maybe it was the feeling that nothing really mattered. She had become complacent without even noticing.
That evening, she sat on the roof with her younger brother. They watched the sunset paint the buildings with ephemeral gold. "Do you think I'm smart?" she asked him. He blinked. "I don't know. But you're kind." Kind. The word made her eyes sting. It felt like a small remnant of hope.
Later, at dinner, her parents talked about the rising cost of flour. Her mother looked tired. Her father looked older. Imani stared at her plate. She felt vulnerable, like a balloon drifting away without string.
That night, she dreamed she was in a huge hall where people were shouting, dancing, singing — a crescendo of chaos — and she was the only one trying to read a book. She woke up feeling melancholy, her heart heavy like soaked cloth.
Over the next week, her emotions fluctuated like the tides. She was happy one morning, then anxious by lunchtime. Sometimes she was elated when a teacher praised her, but the feeling never lasted. She envied friends who seemed stable and focused.
Then came Wednesday. In English class, the teacher asked the students to describe a recent emotional moment in a story. Imani did not raise her hand. But later that day, she began to write. She described her dream. She described the hall and the noise. She added that the book in her hands had no words, only blank pages.
Her teacher, Ms. Alina — who had once worked as a journalist — read the story and clapped. "This must be published in the school paper," she said. "It captures confusion with such candour." Imani felt heat rush to her face. But this time, it was not shame.
That afternoon, as she walked home, she passed a group of older students shouting jokes. One boy was being obnoxious, calling names. Another girl tried to walk away, but he blocked her. Imani hesitated. Then she stepped forward. "Leave her alone." The boy laughed. "You? Little Imani?" But something in her voice had changed. It was not loud — but it was certain. He blinked, shrugged, and left. The girl thanked her softly.

readings.title: A Heart in the Noise, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
That evening, Imani told her mother everything — about the test, the sadness, the story. Her mother listened, then said, "It's easy to be oblivious to what we carry inside. But you're learning." They sat quietly for a long time.
That weekend, the school hosted a debate event. Imani was not planning to go, but her teacher encouraged her. "You don't have to speak," Ms. Alina said. "You can observe. Maybe write something after." So Imani went. She sat at the back of the noisy room while students argued about whether modern society had become more lax or more disciplined.
One boy, dressed in an ostentatious suit, made a bold speech, but his points were shallow. Another girl, though softly spoken, argued with logic and heart. Imani wrote down everything — every flaw, every strength. Her notes became a short article that was published in the school newsletter the following Monday.
Certainly, that was the first time her writing had reached more than ten people. One teacher called the article "surprisingly sophisticated for someone so young." Imani smiled for hours after that.
She started spending more time in the library. She read about emotions, dreams, and young leaders around the world. The shelves were dusty, the chairs askew, but it felt like a second home. In the weeks that followed, she changed — not in a loud, ludicrous way, but slowly, like sunrise.
She still felt nervous at times. She still forgot homework and lost her pencil case now and then. But she also began helping a younger boy in her class who struggled with reading. "You're patient," he told her one afternoon. Imani laughed. "Not always. But I'm trying."
Her friends noticed too. "You seem different," said Sana. "Like... more sure of yourself." "I don't know," Imani replied. "Maybe I'm just more... careful." She now moved through life gingerly, not out of fear but with awareness.
One afternoon, she stayed behind to help clean the classroom. The teacher had left early, and the chairs were stacked in a haphazard pile. Imani slowly arranged them, wiped the board, and straightened the posters. It was nothing major. But it felt good.
At the end of term, she wrote a reflection essay. In it, she described the rollercoaster of feelings she had lived through, and she included a paragraph comparing her past self with her present self. "I used to think that emotion was weakness," she wrote. "But now I see that feeling deeply can be strength — if I learn from it."
Her essay was selected to be read aloud at the school assembly. She stood on the stage, her paper shaking slightly, but her voice was steady. She read until the last sentence, looked up, and saw her mother in the crowd, smiling. The applause that followed was not loud. But it was warm, and it was real. And Imani — who had once felt like a remnant of potential — now felt whole.

comprehension.question: According to 'Moving Through Mogadishu: A City in Motion', what happens on the streets every morning at 6:30?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The streets begin to hum with life: minibuses crowd the main roads, motorcycles weave between cars, and pedestrians walk quickly along the dusty pavements.
comprehension.explanation: Look at the opening picture of the morning rush: the text says the streets "begin to hum with life" as minibuses crowd the main roads, motorcycles weave between cars, and pedestrians walk quickly along dusty pavements.

comprehension.question: In the interview, which two forms of transport does Amara say people mainly use, and when are the buses busiest?
comprehension.correctAnswer: People mainly travel by minibus or bajaaj, and the buses are busiest in the morning and at about 5 p.m., when people are going home from work.
comprehension.explanation: In her first answer Amara says the main way to get around is by minibus or bajaaj, and that the buses are always full "especially in the morning and at about 5 p.m., when people are going home from work".

comprehension.question: What happened at school to make Imani feel so embarrassed at the start of the story?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She scored 37% on her maths test, and her teacher's comment that she must improve her discipline rang in her ears.
comprehension.explanation: In the scene at her mother's kiosk, Imani stares at her crumpled maths test with a red "37%" circled at the top, and her teacher's comment, "You must improve your discipline", rings in her ears.

comprehension.question: What did Imani write down at the debate event, and what happened to her notes afterwards?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She wrote down every flaw and every strength of the speakers, and her notes became a short article that was published in the school newsletter the following Monday.
comprehension.explanation: At the debate, the text says Imani "wrote down everything — every flaw, every strength", and that her notes became a short article published in the school newsletter the following Monday.

comprehension.question: Nadir says, 'A city should not just be built for cars. It should be designed for people.' What does he mean?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He means planners should put the needs of pedestrians and passengers first, designing streets that are safe and easy for everyone to use rather than only making room for traffic.
comprehension.explanation: Nadir is contrasting cars with people. Earlier the text mentions dangerous roads for pedestrians and overcrowded buses, so he means streets should be planned around passengers and walkers being safe and able to navigate easily, not just around traffic.

comprehension.question: Amara begins one answer with 'Unfortunately'. What problems does she describe, and what does that sentence adverb show about her viewpoint?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She describes potholes, dust, roads that flood in the rainy season and the lack of printed maps or timetables, and the adverb shows she regrets these problems and presents them as bad news.
comprehension.explanation: Links the unit's sentence-adverb focus to viewpoint: the adverb signals regret before the evidence arrives.

comprehension.question: Why had Imani stopped studying? Give at least two reasons the story suggests, and explain what the word complacent adds.
comprehension.correctAnswer: The story suggests the noise at home, the way her phone could tempt her away from revising, and the feeling that nothing really mattered; calling her complacent shows she had stopped trying without even noticing it herself.
comprehension.explanation: The text lists three possible causes: the noise at home, her phone tempting her to scroll instead of revising, and the feeling that nothing really mattered. It then says she "had become complacent without even noticing", so she had stopped trying without realising it.

comprehension.correctAnswer: She means people often ignore their own hidden feelings; Imani learns this by telling her mother everything and then writing honestly in her article and her reflection essay.

comprehension.correctAnswer: Support includes roads damaged in years of conflict, minibuses with no fixed timetable, crowded streets and pollution from old vehicles; hope comes from new tarmac and traffic lights, the students' phone-based route map, and the Nairobi and Dar es Salaam projects showing transport problems can be solved.
comprehension.explanation: The text supports the claim with roads damaged in conflict, minibuses that leave only when full, crowded market streets and pollution from old vehicles. Hope comes from new tarmac and traffic lights, the students' phone route map, and Nairobi's mapping project and Dar es Salaam's rapid buses.

comprehension.correctAnswer: Amara is reliable about her own daily journeys because she travels every day, but one commuter cannot speak for a whole city, so traffic counts, the students' route-map data, and interviews with drivers, traders and older passengers would strengthen the picture.
comprehension.explanation: Amara crosses the city every day, so she is a reliable witness to her own journeys, but the closing paragraph admits "one commuter cannot speak for a whole city". Traffic data, the students' route map and other passengers, drivers and traders would give a fuller picture.

comprehension.question: Imani dreams of a huge hall full of shouting and a crescendo of chaos while she holds a book with blank pages. What might the dream symbolise, and how does writing about it change things for her?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The dream suggests she feels lost in noise she cannot control while her own mind stays blank; when she writes about it with candour, Ms. Alina praises the story, and her shame begins to turn into confidence.
comprehension.explanation: In the dream everyone is shouting and dancing in "a crescendo of chaos" while her book has only blank pages, which suggests she feels lost in noise with nothing of her own to say. When she writes about it, Ms. Alina praises its candour and the heat in her face is no longer shame.

comprehension.question: Compare Imani at the beginning of the story with Imani at the end, giving at least three changes and one comparative sentence of your own.
comprehension.correctAnswer: At the start she hides her test, feels vulnerable and has become complacent; by the end she publishes an article, helps a younger reader, tidies the classroom without being asked and reads her essay on stage, so she is more confident, more careful and more generous than before.

By the end she has published an article, helps a younger boy with reading, tidies the classroom unasked and reads her essay on stage, so she is more confident and more careful than before.

grammar.title: Prepositions of Time and Place
grammar.explanation: Prepositions are small but powerful words that show how the other words in a sentence relate to each other, and the three most important prepositions of time and place — in, on and at — make your English sound natural and precise when chosen correctly.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Time: in is for longer periods — months, years, seasons and parts of the day (in January, in 2024, in the morning, in summer). On is for specific days and dates (on Monday, on 5th April, on sports day). At is for exact times and specific moments (at 7 a.m., at noon, at sunset). Exception: we say at night, but in the morning, in the afternoon and in the evening.
Place: in means inside a space — countries, cities, rooms, containers (in Somalia, in the classroom, in the box). On means touching a surface — tables, walls, floors, streets (on the table, on the wall). At marks a specific point — addresses, locations, events (at the bus stop, at the market, at school).
Special phrases to memorise: at the weekend (British English) and on the weekend (American English) are both correct; in a hurry ("She left in a hurry."); in trouble ("He is in trouble."); at first and at last ("At first, I was nervous. At last, I understood."); on time ("The bus arrived on time."); in time ("We arrived just in time for the lesson.").
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: "I will see you in Friday." Fix: "I will see you on Friday." — days take on. Mistake: "I was born at 2012." Fix: "I was born in 2012." — years take in.
grammar.memoryTip: Picture the three words: in means you are inside something (a box, a month, a city); on means you are on top of something (a surface, a day, a date); at means you are at a point (a dot on the map, a moment in time).
grammar.practice:

Part A: 1) at 6 a.m.; 2) in Mogadishu; 3) on Thursday; 4) in the evening; 5) on the wall; 6) at the bus stop; 7) in 2019; 8) on the sofa; 9) at sunset; 10) on 12th August.

grammar.title: Past Simple Passive
grammar.explanation: The past simple passive reports a past event while keeping the focus on what happened rather than on who did it, which suits writing about cities because the roads, bridges and stations usually matter more than their builders.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form it with was (singular) or were (plural) plus the past participle: "The road was built in 2020."; "The traffic lights were installed last month."; "The school was designed by a famous architect."; "New trees were planted along the main street."
Use it when the doer is unknown ("The window was broken last night."), unimportant ("The bridge was completed in March.") or obvious ("The suspect was arrested." — obviously by the police).
To name the doer anyway, add by at the end: "The mural was painted by local artists."; "The road was damaged by heavy rain."
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: "The bridge was build last year." Fix: "The bridge was built last year." — the passive needs the past participle, not the base form. Mistake: "The roads was repaired." Fix: "The roads were repaired." — plural subjects take were.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of the passive as a spotlight: active voice shines the light on the doer, while the past simple passive swings the spotlight onto the thing that received the action.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each active sentence in the past simple passive: 1) Workers built the new school in 2021. 2) The government opened a new hospital last year. 3) Someone stole my bicycle yesterday. 4) The community planted 200 trees along the road. 5) Engineers designed the bridge to carry heavy lorries. 6) A local artist painted the mural on the wall. 7) The storm damaged several buildings in the city. 8) The mayor opened the new bus station on Monday.

— Answer Key —
1) The new school was built in 2021. 2) A new hospital was opened last year. 3) My bicycle was stolen yesterday. 4) 200 trees were planted along the road. 5) The bridge was designed to carry heavy lorries. 6) The mural was painted on the wall. 7) Several buildings were damaged in the city. 8) The new bus station was opened on Monday.
Note: adding "by workers", "by the government", "by a local artist" and so on is optional and still correct — the passive works with or without the by phrase.

grammar.title: Present Simple Passive
grammar.explanation: The present simple passive describes routines and general truths when the focus belongs on the action or the thing receiving it, which is why descriptions of how city services work rely on it so heavily.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form it with is (singular) or are (plural) plus the past participle: "The streets are cleaned every morning."; "Fresh water is delivered to the neighbourhood by lorry."; "Tickets are sold at the station entrance."; "English is spoken in many countries around the world."
Negatives place not after is or are: "The roads are not repaired often enough."; "This street is not used by many cars." Questions move is or are to the front: "Are the buses checked before they leave the station?"; "Is the market opened every day?"
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: "The homework is give by the teacher." Fix: "The homework is given by the teacher." — use the past participle. Mistake: "The books is read by the students." Fix: "The books are read by the students." — plural subjects take are.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask yourself "How is this done?" or "What happens to this?" — if the question makes sense, the present simple passive is probably the form you need.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each active sentence in the present simple passive: 1) The council cleans the streets every week. 2) People speak Somali in many East African countries. 3) The school teaches road safety to young children. 4) Farmers grow rice in the fields near the river. 5) The librarian organises the books every Friday. 6) Workers check the buses before each journey.

— Answer Key —
1) The streets are cleaned every week (by the council). 2) Somali is spoken in many East African countries. 3) Road safety is taught to young children (by the school). 4) Rice is grown in the fields near the river (by farmers).
5) The books are organised every Friday (by the librarian).
6) The buses are checked before each journey (by workers).
Note: the by phrase is optional in every answer; is/are + past participle alone is a complete, correct sentence.

grammar.title: Modal Verbs + Passive Voice
grammar.explanation: Modal verbs such as can, should, must, may and might combine with the passive to say what can be done, should be done or must be done without naming anyone, which makes them the natural language of proposals for improving cities.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form it with a modal verb plus be plus the past participle. Possibility: "Transport problems can be solved with better planning." Obligation: "Old buses must be replaced with cleaner vehicles." Advice: "More trees should be planted in city centres." Permission: "The report may be submitted next week." Possibility again: "Mistakes might be made, but we can learn from them."
Negatives put not after the modal: "The old bridge cannot be used any more."; "Plastic bags should not be thrown in the river."; "This document must not be shared without permission."
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: "The letters must sent by Friday." Fix: "The letters must be sent by Friday." — never drop the be between the modal and the past participle, as in "The road should built next year", which needs "should be built".
grammar.memoryTip: The modal passive is a sandwich: the modal is one slice of bread, the past participle is the other, and be is the filling that can never be left out.
grammar.practice:
Complete each sentence with the correct modal passive form, using the verb in brackets: 1) The new road ______ (should / build) before the rainy season. 2) Old vehicles ______ (must / replace) with cleaner ones. 3) Bus timetables ______ (can / share) on mobile phones. 4) The park ______ (should / clean) every week. 5) This bridge ______ (must / not / use) by heavy lorries. 6) The project ______ (may / complete) by the end of the month. 7) More bicycle lanes ______ (should / create) in the city centre. 8) The rules ______ (must / follow) by everyone.

— Answer Key —
1) should be built; 2) must be replaced; 3) can be shared; 4) should be cleaned; 5) must not be used; 6) may be completed; 7) should be created; 8) must be followed.

grammar.title: Comparative Adjectives and Sentence Adverbs
grammar.explanation: Comparative adjectives set two places, systems or feelings side by side, while sentence adverbs such as fortunately, unfortunately and certainly announce your attitude to the whole sentence — together they power opinion writing about cities.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Comparatives: one-syllable adjectives add -er (fast becomes faster, old becomes older, tall becomes taller); one-syllable adjectives ending consonant-vowel-consonant double the last letter (big becomes bigger, hot becomes hotter); two-syllable adjectives ending in -y change -y to -i and add -er (busy becomes busier, noisy becomes noisier, happy becomes happier); longer adjectives take more (more crowded, more beautiful, more dangerous); irregulars are learned by heart (good becomes better, bad becomes worse, far becomes farther or further). Always use than when naming both things: "Nairobi is bigger than Hargeisa."; "Buses are cheaper than taxis."; "Cycling is more environmentally friendly than driving."
Comparatives also describe feelings, as in the story: "She feels more vulnerable than before."; "Imani became more confident as the term went on."; "The second speech was better than the first."
Sentence adverbs sit at the start or end of a sentence, set off by a comma: fortunately for good news ("Fortunately, the bus arrived just in time."), unfortunately for bad news ("Unfortunately, the road was closed."), certainly for confidence ("The city has certainly improved.").
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: "Unfortunately we missed the bus." Fix: "Unfortunately, we missed the bus." — the comma after the adverb is required. Mistake: "Unfortunately, it was a wonderful day." Fix: "Fortunately, it was a wonderful day." — unfortunately introduces bad news, not good.
grammar.memoryTip: Remember F-C-U — Fortunately for good news, Certainly for agreement, Unfortunately for bad news — and let the comma after each one act as a small drum roll before the rest of your sentence.
grammar.practice:
Part A — write the correct comparative form: 1) This city is ______ (noisy) than my village. 2) The train is ______ (fast) than the bus. 3) Her essay was ______ (good) than mine. 4) The old market is ______ (crowded) than the new one. 5) He felt ______ (vulnerable) after the incident. 6) Walking is ______ (slow) than cycling.
Part B — add fortunately, unfortunately or certainly: 7) ______, the bridge collapsed during the storm and no one could cross. 8) ______, no one was hurt in the accident. 9) The new bus service has ______ made travel easier for everyone. 10) ______, I left my bag on the bus and it was gone when I returned.
Part C — more comparatives: 11) Dar es Salaam is ______ (hot) than Nairobi. 12) A bicycle is ______ (cheap) than a car. 13) This route is ______ (dangerous) than the main road. 14) The new bus is ______ (comfortable) than the old one. 15) Walking is ______ (slow) than taking the bus. 16) Mogadishu is ______ (busy) than my village.
Part D — more sentence adverbs: 17) ______, we missed the last bus and had to walk home. 18) ______, a kind driver stopped and offered us a lift. 19) The new bicycle lanes have ______ made the city safer. 20) ______, the bridge was closed for repairs during rush hour.

— Answer Key —
Part A: 1) noisier; 2) faster; 3) better; 4) more crowded; 5) more vulnerable; 6) slower.
Part B: 7) Unfortunately; 8) Fortunately; 9) certainly; 10) Unfortunately.
Part C: 11) hotter; 12) cheaper; 13) more dangerous; 14) more comfortable; 15) slower; 16) busier.
Part D: 17) Unfortunately; 18) Fortunately; 19) certainly; 20) Unfortunately.
Self-check: fortunately/unfortunately/certainly at the very start of a sentence always needs a comma right after it (items 7, 8, 10, 17, 18, 20); used in the middle of a sentence (items 9 and 19), no comma is needed.

grammar.title: Grade 7 Editing and Application
grammar.explanation: Strong writers pull the unit's four grammar focuses together, moving between prepositions, passives, comparatives and sentence adverbs while revising whole paragraphs for meaning, accuracy and flow.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Work through a paragraph one feature at a time: first check every preposition of time and place, then confirm each passive uses the right form of be plus a past participle, then test each comparative for -er or more plus than, and finally check every sentence adverb carries its comma. Reading the paragraph aloud after each pass catches the errors your eyes slide over, and explaining the purpose of a revision proves that it genuinely improved the writing.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: changing words without checking whether the paragraph still means the same thing. Fix: reread after every edit and explain the purpose of each revision in one sentence.
grammar.memoryTip: Edit the way a mechanic services a bus: one system at a time — prepositions, passives, comparatives, adverbs — then take the whole paragraph for a test drive by reading it aloud.
grammar.practice:
Part A — rewrite in the passive: 1) The government built a new hospital in the city centre. 2) Workers repair the roads every summer. 3) The community should plant more trees along the main road. 4) Engineers designed the bridge to carry heavy traffic. 5) Local artists can paint murals on empty walls. 6) The school teaches road safety to young children.
Part B — write a comparative sentence from the notes: 7) buses / taxis (cheap). 8) Nairobi / my village (crowded). 9) the new road / the old road (smooth). 10) cycling / driving (environmentally friendly). 11) morning traffic / evening traffic (bad). 12) this neighbourhood / that neighbourhood (quiet).
Part C — write six sentences of your own about transport or city life: two using a preposition of time or place, two using any passive form, and two using a comparative adjective or a sentence adverb.
Part D — edit a four-paragraph draft of your travel guide: mark eight changes and explain how four of them improve clarity and cohesion.

— Answer Key —
Part A: 1) A new hospital was built in the city centre. 2) The roads are repaired every summer. 3) More trees should be planted along the main road. 4) The bridge was designed to carry heavy traffic. 5) Murals can be painted on empty walls. 6) Road safety is taught to young children.
Part B: 7) Buses are cheaper than taxis. 8) Nairobi is more crowded than my village. 9) The new road is smoother than the old road. 10) Cycling is more environmentally friendly than driving. 11) Morning traffic is worse than evening traffic. 12) This neighbourhood is quieter than that neighbourhood.
Part C is open-ended (your own sentences), so there is no single correct answer — use this model to self-check instead: "Fortunately, the new bicycle lanes are checked every month, and they are safer than the old road." Confirm your two preposition sentences use in/on/at correctly for time or place, your two passive sentences use is/am/are/was/were + past participle, and your two comparative/adverb sentences use -er or more + than, or open with fortunately/unfortunately/certainly followed by a comma.
Part D refers to a four-paragraph draft that is not printed in this exercise, so there is no fixed answer to check against either. Self-check your own draft using the rule above instead: reread it once for each of the four grammar focuses in this unit — prepositions (in/on/at chosen correctly), passive voice (right form of be + past participle), comparatives (-er/more + than), and sentence adverbs (comma after fortunately/unfortunately/certainly when they open a sentence) — then write one sentence for each of your four chosen edits explaining how it improved clarity or cohesion.

writing.promptAndInstructions: Plan and write a travel guide for a city you know or would like to visit — Mogadishu, Nairobi, Dar es Salaam, Hargeisa, Kampala, or an imaginary city you design yourself. Plan first: where the city is, what it is famous for, how people travel around it, what the food is like, and the best time to visit. Then write four to five paragraphs: an introduction that uses one passive sentence (for example, "The city was founded centuries ago."); a getting-around section that compares two forms of transport with a comparative adjective; a section on what to see and do; a challenges-and-hopes section that opens with a sentence adverb; and a closing recommendation. Use prepositions of time and place correctly throughout, and include at least five unit vocabulary words.
writing.modelText:
Mogadishu was built centuries ago beside the Indian Ocean, and today it hums with contemporary energy and busy markets.
Minibuses are more affordable than taxis, though a bajaaj moves more quickly through narrow, crowded streets, and fares can fluctuate during rush hour.
Visitors can walk gingerly along the crowded beach at sunset or explore the old market, where traders sell spices and sophisticated jewellery.
Unfortunately, some roads are still under repair, but fortunately new tarmac is laid monthly, and the city feels formidable in its rebuilding.
I recommend visiting in the cool months, when the streets are calm before the evening crowds arrive.

items: Paragraph 1 (introduction, passive sentence): Nairobi was founded in the late nineteenth century as a small railway depot, and today it has grown into a sophisticated, contemporary capital full of glass towers and busy matatus.

Paragraph 2 (getting around, comparative adjective): Matatus are more affordable than private taxis, though a taxi moves more quickly through the city's notorious traffic jams, and fares can fluctuate depending on the time of day.

Paragraph 3 (what to see and do): Visitors can walk gingerly through the crowded stalls of the city market, where traders sell sophisticated jewellery and fresh coffee, or explore the nearby national park, where giraffes wander within sight of the skyline.

Paragraph 4 (challenges and hopes, opens with a sentence adverb): Unfortunately, some neighbourhoods still struggle with formidable traffic and unreliable electricity, but fortunately new train lines are being built every year, and residents remain hopeful about the city's future.
Paragraph 5 (closing recommendation): I recommend visiting in the cool, dry season, when the jacaranda trees bloom along the avenues and the streets feel calmer before the evening rush begins.

writing.title: Writing 2: A Diary Entry for Imani

writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine you are Imani on the evening after Ms. Alina praised your story in "A Heart in the Noise". Write her diary entry for that night. Dear diary,
Today Ms. Alina read my story aloud, and for the first time in weeks I felt truly elated instead of melancholy. My hands were shaking, but her kind words melted my doubt.
Certainly, I still feel a little vulnerable about sharing more of my writing, but fortunately I know now that people want to hear it. Tomorrow I will show Mum the story too.

items: Dear diary, today Ms. Alina read my story aloud to the whole class, and for the first time in weeks I felt truly elated instead of melancholy. My hands were shaking so much that I almost dropped my pencil, but her kind words melted every doubt I had been carrying.

Certainly, I still feel a little vulnerable about sharing more of my writing with people who barely know me, but fortunately I now understand that my classmates actually want to hear what I have to say, not just laugh at me the way I feared.
I keep replaying the moment when the whole room went quiet and then clapped, and it makes the maths test I failed last week feel much smaller than it did this morning.
Tomorrow I will show Mum the story too, and maybe I will even ask Ms. Alina whether I can enter it into the school journal, because tonight, for once, I actually believe it is good enough.

writing.title: Writing 4: Reflect and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Return to your city travel guide and edit it against this checklist: at least two passive sentences; at least two comparative adjectives; at least one sentence adverb used correctly; prepositions of time and place checked; at least five unit vocabulary words; every sentence capitalised and punctuated. writing.modelText: My first draft said the city has good transport, which was vague and included no unit vocabulary. I revised it to: fares can fluctuate during rush hour, and minibuses are more affordable than taxis, which is more precise and includes a comparative adjective. I also checked my prepositions, adding along the beach and beside the ocean, and confirmed that the market was visited by traders and new tarmac is laid monthly. Fortunately, the biggest improvement was adding contemporary, sophisticated details, because those formidable images helped my reader picture Mogadishu clearly.

items: Revisions: Before: "The transport is good." After: "Matatus are more affordable than private taxis, though fares can fluctuate depending on the time of day." Before: "There is a market." After: "Visitors can walk gingerly through the crowded stalls of the city market, where traders sell sophisticated jewellery." Before: "Some roads have problems." After: "Unfortunately, some neighbourhoods still struggle with formidable traffic, but fortunately new train lines are being built every year."

Reflection: The improvement that helped my writing most was adding precise details and comparative language instead of vague words like "good" and "problems". writing.title: Writing 5: City and Emotion

writing.promptAndInstructions: The story is set in a noisy, busy neighbourhood. Write a description of a noisy, busy place you know — a market, a bus station, or a playground at break time. Vendors call out prices beside the road, and passengers wait, gingerly stepping around puddles, some elated to be going home and others wary of missing their bus. writing.title: Writing 6: Debate Verdict — Cars or Public Transport?
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: After the class debate about whether cities should build more roads for cars or invest in better public transport, write your verdict. State which side you agree with, give two reasons supported by evidence from the unit texts, answer one argument from the other side, and close with a recommendation for your own city. Use at least one sentence adverb and one comparative adjective, and organise your verdict into clear paragraphs.
writing.modelText: I agree that our city should invest in better public transport rather than more roads for cars. First, as Amara explained, minibuses already form a formidable network that carries far more people than private cars, helping more passengers at once. Second, Mogadishu's roads are still being rebuilt, and wider roads would only tempt more haphazard traffic into the same crowded streets. Some argue that cars are more comfortable, but comfort matters less than getting everyone to work and school safely. Certainly, our city should spend its money on cheaper, more reliable buses for everyone.

items: I agree that our city should invest in better public transport rather than building more roads for cars. First, as one debate speaker explained, minibuses already form a formidable network that carries far more passengers at once than private cars ever could on the same street.
Second, many of our roads are still being repaired, and building wider roads would only tempt more haphazard traffic onto streets that are already crowded rather than solving the real problem.

Some students argued that cars are more comfortable than buses, and that may be true for a single passenger, but comfort matters less than getting hundreds of people to school and work safely every single day.
Certainly, our city should spend its money on cheaper, more reliable buses for everyone, because a transport system that only serves people who can afford a car leaves too many families behind.
otherAnswers: A learner who agreed with building more roads for cars might argue that new roads reduce congestion for ambulances and delivery trucks, and that public transport alone cannot reach every neighbourhood.
A learner arguing for cars might answer the public-transport side by pointing out that buses do not run late at night, leaving shift workers with no safe way home.
A learner could also propose a middle position: build a small number of new roads for emergency vehicles while still investing most of the budget in buses.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Transport, Cities, and Urban Solutions" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 11-12 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'melancholy'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "Moving Through Mogadishu: A City in Motion" was about in their own words, and what happened in "A Heart in the Noise, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Prepositions of Time and Place" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.
